chapters.n: Paul opens his letter with Timothy at his side, writing to the whole branch of Saints in Philippi and their local leaders. Philippi was a Roman colony in Macedonia and the first place in Europe where Paul planted the gospel.

f.g: Local Church officers: “bishops” (Greek episkopoi, overseers) presided; deacons (diakonoi) served under them.

chapters.n: Paul’s usual greeting blends the Greek “grace” (God’s unearned help and favor) with the Hebrew “peace” (shalom, wholeness). Both come from the Father and the Son together.

f.g: Greek charis — gift, favor, divine enabling help.

chapters.n: Every time Paul thinks of the Philippians, it turns into gratitude. This is one of his warmest letters; the Philippians had supported him faithfully for years.
His prayers for them are not anxious or heavy but full of joy. “Joy” and “rejoice” run through this letter more than any other Paul wrote, even though he writes from prison.
“Fellowship” means partnership. From the day Lydia was baptized, the Philippians had shared in Paul’s work with their faith, prayers, and money.

f.g: Greek koinōnia — sharing, partnership, common participation.

chapters.n: Paul is sure that God, who started a good work in them, will keep working until it is finished at Christ’s Second Coming. God does not abandon a work He begins in a willing heart.

f.g: The Second Coming, when Christ returns in glory to judge and reign.

chapters.n: It is fitting (“meet”) for Paul to feel this way because he holds them in his heart. Whether he is in chains or defending the gospel in court, they share with him in the same grace.
Paul calls God as his witness that he longs for them with the very tenderness of Christ. In KJV English the “bowels” were considered the seat of deep feeling, as we would say “the heart.”

f.g: Inward affections, deep compassion — the heart.

chapters.n: His prayer is that their love will keep growing, guided by real knowledge and wise discernment. Love without understanding can be misdirected; Paul wants both together.
With discerning love they can recognize and choose what is truly best, and live with pure motives, not causing others to stumble, until Christ comes.

f.g: Greek eilikrinēs — pure, unmixed; tested in sunlight and found genuine.
Not stumbling and not causing others to stumble.

chapters.n: The good fruit in their lives comes through Jesus Christ, and all of it brings glory to God. Righteousness here is not self-made but grows from being connected to Christ.
Paul wants them to know that his imprisonment has not stopped the gospel; it has actually helped it spread. Hardship became an opportunity.
Everyone in the “palace” — likely the Praetorian Guard, the emperor’s elite soldiers who took turns guarding Paul — now knows he is a prisoner because of Christ, not for a crime.

f.g: Greek praitōrion — the Praetorian Guard or the governor’s headquarters.

chapters.n: Seeing Paul’s courage in chains, many other believers have grown bolder in sharing the gospel. His example strengthened them instead of scaring them.
Not everyone preaching Christ has good motives. Some are driven by jealousy and rivalry toward Paul; others preach out of genuine goodwill.
The rivals preach to compete with Paul, hoping to make his imprisonment more painful by outshining or embarrassing him.
The others preach out of love, understanding that Paul has been appointed to defend the gospel and supporting that mission.
Paul’s remarkable response: what matters most is that Christ is being preached, whatever the motive. He refuses to let personal rivalry steal his joy.
Paul trusts that their prayers and the help of the Spirit of Christ will bring about his deliverance — whether release from prison or ultimate salvation.

f.g: Greek sōtēria — rescue, deliverance; possibly here release from prison.

chapters.n: His deepest hope is never to shrink back in shame, but to honor Christ by how he lives — or by how he dies, if it comes to that.

f.g: Made great, honored, shown to be glorious.

chapters.n: One of Paul’s most famous lines: his whole life is about Christ, and death would only bring him closer to Christ. Either way, he cannot lose.
If he keeps living, that means more fruitful work for the Lord. So he honestly does not know which he would choose.
Paul feels pulled in two directions. Part of him longs to leave mortality and be with Christ, which would be far better for him personally.

f.g: A tight place; hard-pressed between two choices.
Greek analuō — to loosen, as in breaking camp or untying a ship to set sail.

chapters.n: But staying alive is more needed for the Saints’ sake. Paul puts their spiritual needs ahead of his own desire for rest.
Paul feels confident that he will remain alive and continue serving them so their faith can grow and bring them joy.
When he comes back to visit them, their rejoicing in Christ will overflow. Many believe Paul was indeed released from this first Roman imprisonment.
Whatever happens to Paul, they should live in a way worthy of the gospel, standing together in unity of spirit and purpose, like a team striving side by side.

f.g: Way of life, conduct. Greek politeuesthe — live as citizens, a fitting word for a Roman colony.
Contending side by side, like athletes or soldiers.

chapters.n: Do not be frightened by opponents. Their hostility is a sign that they are on the path to ruin, while your courage is evidence that God is saving you.

f.g: Startled, spooked — like a frightened horse.

chapters.n: Paul presents suffering for Christ as a privilege “given” to them, a gift alongside the gift of faith. Disciples share in their Lord’s experiences.
The Philippians had seen Paul beaten and jailed in their own city, and now hear of his Roman chains. They face the same kind of struggle he does.

f.g: Greek agōn — struggle, contest, as in an athletic arena.

chapters.n: Paul appeals to everything they have received: if Christ has ever encouraged you, if love has comforted you, if the Spirit has bound you together, if you have felt tenderness and mercy — then act on it.
Make my joy complete by being united: one in love, one in heart, one in purpose. Unity among the Saints was Paul’s greatest wish for this beloved branch.
Don’t act out of rivalry or a desire to look important. Instead, humbly treat others as more important than yourself.

f.g: Empty conceit, seeking praise for oneself.

chapters.n: Don’t look out only for your own interests; care about other people’s needs too. This sets up Paul’s great example of Christ.
Have the same attitude Jesus had. Verses 6–11 are often called the “Christ hymn” — many scholars think it was an early Christian hymn or poem Paul quotes.

f.w: Let this mind be in you
f.g: Think the way Christ thought; adopt His attitude.

chapters.n: Though Christ shared the divine nature with the Father in the premortal life, He did not cling to that status as something to hold onto for Himself.

f.g: Greek morphē — true nature, not just outward look.
Something to grasp or cling to. Christ’s equality with God was rightly His, yet He did not grasp it selfishly.

chapters.n: Instead He emptied Himself, taking the lowly role of a servant and being born as a human being. Latter-day Saints call this the condescension of God.
As a man, He humbled Himself even further — obeying the Father all the way to death, and not just any death, but crucifixion, the most shameful execution Rome used.

f.g: Crucifixion was reserved for slaves and rebels; it was meant to shame.

chapters.n: Because of that humility, the Father lifted Christ to the highest place and gave Him the greatest of all names. The way down became the way up.

f.w: a name which is above every name

chapters.n: Every being — in heaven, on earth, and among the dead — will eventually bow before Jesus. Paul is echoing Isaiah, where Jehovah says every knee shall bow to Him.
And everyone will acknowledge that Jesus Christ is Lord, which brings glory to the Father. Christ’s exaltation honors the Father rather than competing with Him.

f.g: Greek kyrios — the word the Greek Old Testament used for Jehovah.

chapters.n: So, just as you have always obeyed, keep at it even more now that I’m not there: work out your salvation with reverent seriousness. Salvation is a gift, but disciples must actively live it out.

f.g: Deep reverence and humility, not terror.

chapters.n: You are not working alone — God is working in you, giving you both the desire and the power to do what pleases Him. Our effort and His grace work together.

f.w: both to will and to do

chapters.n: Do everything without grumbling or arguing. Complaining divides communities, and Paul wants this branch united.
Then you will be pure and innocent children of God, shining like stars in a dark and twisted world. Paul echoes Moses’s words about a crooked generation.
Hold out the life-giving message of the gospel to others. Then, at Christ’s coming, Paul can rejoice that his efforts — his race and labor — were not wasted.
Even if Paul’s life is poured out like a drink offering on top of their faith-offering, he is glad. He pictures his possible death as a sacrifice added to theirs.

f.g: Greek spendomai — poured out like a drink offering (libation) on a sacrifice.

chapters.n: Paul invites them to share his joy rather than mourn for him. Rejoicing together becomes a bond between them.
Paul hopes, if the Lord wills, to send Timothy soon so that he can hear how they are doing and be encouraged by good news.

f.g: How you are doing; your circumstances.

chapters.n: No one else shares Paul’s heart the way Timothy does, or cares so genuinely for their welfare.
Paul laments that most people are focused on their own concerns rather than on Christ’s work. Timothy is a happy exception.
The Philippians already know Timothy’s proven character; he has served alongside Paul like a son working with his father.

f.w: as a son with the father

chapters.n: Paul plans to send Timothy as soon as he learns the outcome of his own trial.
Paul trusts the Lord that he himself will soon be released and come visit them.
Meanwhile, he is sending Epaphroditus — a Philippian whom the branch had sent to bring Paul gifts and care for him. Paul honors him with three titles: brother, co-worker, and fellow soldier.

f.g: Greek apostolos — one sent on a mission.

chapters.n: Epaphroditus was homesick and distressed — not about his own illness, but because the Philippians had heard about it and would worry.
He had nearly died. But God showed mercy by healing him, sparing Paul from adding grief upon grief to his imprisonment.
So Paul is sending him home eagerly, so the Philippians can rejoice to see him well and Paul can have one less worry.
Welcome him joyfully as a brother in the Lord, and honor people like him who serve so selflessly.
He risked his life doing Christ’s work, filling in the service the Philippians could not give in person because they were far away.

f.g: Some manuscripts read “gambling with his life.”
What you were unable to do yourselves because of distance — not a criticism.

chapters.n: Paul returns to his theme: rejoice in the Lord. He doesn’t mind repeating his warnings, because repetition keeps them safe.
Paul sharply warns against false teachers who insisted Gentile converts must be circumcised. He turns their own insults back on them: they are the “dogs” and their cutting is mere “mutilation.”

f.g: Some Jews called Gentiles “dogs”; Paul reverses the label onto those teaching a false gospel.

chapters.n: True covenant people — the real “circumcision” — are those who worship by the Spirit, glory in Christ, and do not rely on outward rituals or human credentials.

f.g: Outward human status or physical rites.

chapters.n: If anyone could boast in religious credentials, Paul could — and more than his critics. He lists his own impressive record to make a point.
Paul’s pedigree was flawless: circumcised on schedule, an Israelite by birth, from Benjamin’s respected tribe, raised speaking Hebrew, and a Pharisee — the strictest party in obeying the law.
His zeal was so great that he persecuted the Church, and by the standard of outward law-keeping, no one could fault him.
But all those advantages that he once counted as profit, he now writes off as loss compared to Christ. Paul uses the language of an accountant balancing a ledger.
In fact, Paul considers everything rubbish compared to the surpassing worth of knowing Christ. He has truly lost everything for Him, and counts it nothing in order to gain Christ.

f.g: Greek skybala — refuse, garbage, dung; a deliberately strong word.

chapters.n: Paul wants to be found united with Christ, not trusting a righteousness he earned by keeping rules, but the righteousness God gives through faith in Christ.

f.w: the righteousness which is of God by faith

chapters.n: Paul’s heart’s desire: to know Christ personally — to feel the power of His Resurrection, to share in His sufferings, and to become like Him even in death.
His goal is to reach the glorious resurrection of the righteous. “If by any means” expresses humble longing, not doubt.
Paul admits he has not yet arrived or become complete. But he keeps pressing on to take hold of the purpose for which Christ took hold of him on the Damascus road.
Like a runner in a race, he doesn’t look back at past achievements or failures. He focuses forward, stretching toward what lies ahead.

f.w: forgetting those things which are behind

chapters.n: He presses toward the finish line to win the prize: God’s heavenly call in Christ — eternal life with Him.
Those who are spiritually mature should share this forward-looking attitude. If anyone sees things differently, God will make it clear to them in time.
Meanwhile, let us live up to whatever level of understanding we have already reached, staying on the same path together.
Paul invites them to imitate him together and to watch those who live by the pattern he set.
With tears, Paul warns again about people who live as enemies of Christ’s cross — rejecting the self-sacrifice it represents.

f.w: enemies of the cross of Christ

chapters.n: Their path leads to ruin. Their appetites are their god, they take pride in what should shame them, and their minds are fixed only on worldly things.

By contrast, our true citizenship is in heaven. Philippi’s residents were proud Roman citizens; Paul reminds the Saints that their deeper loyalty is to a heavenly kingdom, and they await their King from there.
When Christ comes, He will transform our weak, humble bodies into resurrected bodies like His own glorious body, by the same power with which He rules all things.

f.g: Body of humiliation — lowly, not wicked.

f.w: fashioned like unto his glorious body

chapters.n: Paul pours out his affection: the Philippians are his joy and his victory wreath. Because of all he has taught, they should stand firm in the Lord.

f.g: Greek stephanos — the victor’s wreath awarded to winning athletes.

chapters.n: Paul gently names two women leaders in the branch, Euodias and Syntyche, and urges them to settle their disagreement and be united in the Lord.
He asks a trusted partner (“true yokefellow,” possibly a person’s name) to help these women reconcile. They had worked hard beside Paul, and their names are written in God’s book of life.

f.g: Companion yoked together in work; some think it was a proper name, Syzygus.

chapters.n: Rejoice in the Lord always — and Paul says it twice for emphasis. This command comes from a man in chains, showing that gospel joy does not depend on circumstances.
Let everyone see that you are gentle and reasonable. The Lord is near — both close beside you and coming soon.
Don’t be anxious about anything. Instead, bring every concern to God in prayer, with thanksgiving.

f.g: Don’t be anxious or worried about anything.

chapters.n: Then God’s peace — a peace deeper than human reasoning can explain — will stand guard over your heart and mind through Christ.

f.g: Greek phroureō — guard, as a garrison guards a city.

chapters.n: Fill your mind with what is true, honorable, right, pure, lovely, and praiseworthy. Joseph Smith echoed this verse in the thirteenth article of faith.
Put into practice what you learned from Paul’s teaching and his example, and the God of peace will be with you. Thinking good things (v. 8) must lead to doing them.
Paul thanks them for their renewed support. They had always cared, but had not had a chance to show it until now.

f.g: Blossomed again, like a plant in spring.

chapters.n: Paul isn’t complaining about being in need; he has learned to be content in any situation.

f.g: Greek autarkēs — self-sufficient, at peace with what one has.

chapters.n: He has known both poverty and plenty, hunger and fullness. He has learned the “secret” of handling either with faith.

f.g: Greek memyēmai — initiated into a secret.

chapters.n: The secret is Christ: Paul can face anything through the One who gives him strength. In context, “all things” especially means enduring both hardship and abundance.
Even so, Paul tells them they did well to share in his troubles by helping him.
From the beginning, when Paul first left Macedonia, the Philippians were the only branch to partner with him financially.

f.g: A business phrase for a shared account — a partnership.

chapters.n: Even while he was in nearby Thessalonica, they sent help more than once.
Paul isn’t fishing for more gifts. He cares about the blessings that will be credited to their account before God because of their generosity.

f.g: Accrue to your credit, like interest.

chapters.n: He has more than enough now that Epaphroditus has arrived with their gifts. He calls their giving a fragrant offering that pleases God, like temple sacrifices.

f.w: an odour of a sweet smell

chapters.n: Just as they supplied Paul’s needs, God will supply all of theirs from His glorious riches in Christ.
A short burst of praise: glory to God our Father forever.
Paul sends greetings to every Saint and passes on greetings from his companions.
All the Saints send greetings — especially converts in “Caesar’s household,” meaning servants and officials in the imperial administration. The gospel had reached the heart of Rome.

f.g: The emperor’s staff of slaves, freedmen and officials, not necessarily his family.

chapters.n: Paul closes as he opened, with grace — the gift of Christ’s help and favor for all of them.
